title: Annotated Direct Explanation of the True Mind
author: Zhanran (commentary)
excerpt: Seek not the Buddha far on Vulture Peak; the Vulture Peak is right within your mind;

inline.s: Course
Textbook
Written by National Master Bojo Chinul of Goryeo
Seek not the Buddha far on Vulture Peak; / The Vulture Peak is in your mind to seek.
Each person has a Vulture Peak tower; / There cultivate, hour by hour.
Recognize the dharmakaya, not the physical body;
Recognize the numinous knowing, not deluded thoughts.
One who awakens to this and guards it sits in the single suchness and attains unmoving liberation;
One who is deluded and turns from it drifts through the six realms and circles through long eons.
[The Vulture Peak is right in your mind]
The Sixth Patriarch said:

'The physical body of the ordinary person is a city; the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are its gates. Outside there are five gates, and within there is the mind-gate. The mind is the ground and the nature is the king; the king dwells upon the ground of the mind. When the nature is present, the king is present; when the nature departs, the king is gone. When the nature is present, body and mind survive; when the nature departs, body and mind are destroyed. The Buddha is realized within the nature; do not seek him outside the body. When the self-nature is deluded, that is the sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha.'
(see
Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
The Flower Garland Sutra
Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathagata says:
'There is not one sentient being that does not fully possess the Tathagata's wisdom; but because of false thinking and inverted attachments, they fail to realize it;
if they abandon false thinking
, then the wisdom of all things, the natural wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom all become manifest now.'
if one abandons false thinking

There are three levels here: the coarse thought ceases, the subtle thought ceases, and then even the extremely subtle thought ceases. For example, for a reciter of the Buddha's name, false thoughts are the coarse thought, while the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is the subtle thought. Ordinarily, when both coarse and subtle thoughts have subsided, this is called no-thought; this is no-thought as generally spoken of. Going further, if even the extremely subtle thought also stops, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore, the meaning of the term no-thought must be determined according to its context. [Extremely subtle thought] The extremely subtle arising and ceasing and flowing of the cognitive mind is an aspect of the alayavijnana (store consciousness). The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
'When the bodhisattva's stage is exhausted
(having fully fulfilled the ten stages)
, satisfying the expedient means, in a single thought corresponding, the mind of awakening first arises, and the mind has no initial aspect;
because of being apart from extremely subtle thought,
one sees the mind-nature,
and the mind is then ever-abiding,
which is called ultimate awakening
Master Guifeng said:
'If the extremely subtle flowing stream
(the extremely subtle thought)

is entirely stilled, only the great wisdom of perfect awakening stands alone, bright and clear; then according with circumstances it manifests hundreds of billions of bodies to save sentient beings of karmic connection,
and this is called being a Buddha
(See the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era.)

[Wisdom of all things] Of all inner dharmas and inner names, it can know and understand; of all outer dharmas and outer names, it too can know and understand. [Natural wisdom] The wisdom that arises of itself, with no reliance on applied effort. [Unobstructed wisdom] The wisdom that is freely unobstructed, that is, the Buddha's wisdom.
The Surangama Sutra says:
'All sentient beings, from beginningsless time, in the continuity of birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind as the pure and bright essence of the nature,
(that is, because they do not know that their abiding in the true mind is this pure and bright essence of the nature)
, they employ a multitude of false thoughts
(and because they employ false thoughts)
; these thoughts are not true, and therefore there is transmigration.'

[True mind as pure and bright essence of nature] Pure and bright essence of nature is the bright, wondrous essence whose nature is originally pure. From the grammatical structure, pure and bright essence of nature is an appositive, used to modify the noun true mind. [Transmigration] The birth-and-death of delimited divisions and the birth-and-death of transformation. [Birth-and-death of delimited divisions] Among sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of what their wholesome and unwholesome karma produces, their lifespans all have limits and their physical forms all have separate sections; hence their birth-and-death is called birth-and-death of delimited divisions. One who is liberated from birth-and-death of delimited divisions escapes the wheel of transmigration. [Birth-and-death of transformation] The noble ones of the three vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and attachment and transcended the birth-and-death of delimited divisions, in the course of cultivation their deluded thoughts gradually cease and their realization gradually grows. This transition from delusion to awakening differs in each stage; as one moves from an earlier stage to a later one, it is just like one death and rebirth, and its transformation is so subtle and unfathomable that it is inconceivable; hence it is called birth-and-death of transformation. One who is liberated from the birth-and-death of transformation fully realizes Buddhahood.
Master Guifeng said:

'All dharmas are like a dream, as all the noble ones alike declare. Therefore false thoughts are originally still, and the realms of dust are originally empty. The empty, still mind is numinous knowing, never dimmed.
This very empty and still knowing is your true nature.

. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind is originally self-aware; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it arise because of objects. This single word knowing is the gate to all wonders. Because of delusion from beginnings, we falsely grasp body and mind as self and give rise to thoughts of greed and hatred. If one obtains the guidance of a good friend and suddenly awakens to this empty, still knowing, this knowing is without thought and without form, then who is the sign of self and the sign of person? Awakening that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately awaken; when awakened, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here. Thus, though one may perfectly cultivate myriad practices, one takes no-thought as the sole essence. Once one has the view of no-thought, then love and aversion naturally become faint, compassion and wisdom naturally grow bright, karmic offenses naturally cease, and meritorious practice naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are no-mark, there is naturally the cultivation of no-cultivation. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are extinguished. When arising and ceasing have ceased, still illumination appears before one, applied without end; this is called being Buddha.'
(From the Preface to the Collection of the Various Commentaries on the Sources of Chan.)
empty, still knowing

also called numinous knowing. [Awakening that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately awaken; when awakened, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here.] Awakening that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a false thought arises, one must immediately awaken to the fact that one is taking illusion to be real and being turned by illusory marks. Once one awakens to this, the false thought immediately vanishes. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies right here!

inline.s: A brief introduction to National Master Bojo:
Chinul (
, roughly the Southern Song period in China), also written Zhinu (
ne

), the founding patriarch of the Korean Jogye Order. A native of Dongju in Gyeongseo (Seoheung County, Hwanghae Province), he went by the style name the Oxherder. His lay surname was Zheng. At the age of eight he left home under Priest Jonghwi of Jogyesan. After receiving the full precepts, he formed a society with more than ten fellow students to practice concentration and wisdom. At twenty-five he passed the monastic examination and resided at Cheongwon Temple in Changpyeong, where he had an awakening through reading the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. At twenty-eight he moved to Pumun Temple at Hagasan, where he obtained Li Tongxuan's Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra (the New Avatamsaka Commentary) of the Tang dynasty, and realized that the essential teaching of Chan accords with the doctrine of the Avatamsaka. Later, at Geojosa temple on Palgongsan, he composed the Cultivation of Concentration and Wisdom Society Letter to spur himself on in actual practice. After several years he retired to Muju Hermitage on Jirisan, devoted entirely to inner contemplation. One day, reading the Record of Dahui, he suddenly had a great awakening. In the third year of the reign of King Sinjong (

), he again formed a society at Gilseong Temple on Songgwangsan, and over some eleven years devoted himself to spreading Jogye Chan, advocating immediate awakening followed by gradual cultivation, and the equal maintenance of concentration and wisdom. Afterward he founded the White Cloud Retreat on Ibosang, the Jipseok Hermitage, the Joyang Hermitage, and others. In the first year of King Huijong (
), he changed Jeonghye Temple on Songgwangsan into the Jogyesan Cultivation Society, which became the fundamental center of Korean Zen.
In the sixth year of King Huijong (

), in spring, the master knew the time of his passing had come. On the night before his nirvana, while he was bathing, an attendant kept asking him questions; the master answered each one calmly. At dawn the next day (on the twenty-seventh day of the third month), everyone came to see him off. The master had the attendant strike the drum to gather the assembly, and, staff in hand, he strode briskly into the Dharma hall, ascended the seat, and gave a lecture. He said: 'The efficacy of Chan is inconceivable. Today, having come here, I intend to set forth clearly this inconceivable mystery for you. Whoever wishes may now come up and ask; I, this old man, will surely answer you one by one.' Everyone began to ask questions, and the master responded according to each, with unobstructed eloquence. Having answered the final question, he tapped his staff on the ground several times and said: 'Say a thousand words, say ten thousand words, all of it is right here.' Having spoken, he sat serenely and passed away tranquilly.

The master lived to fifty-three, with a Dharma age of thirty-six; his posthumous title was National Master Buddha-Sun Bojo. He authored the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, the Cultivation of Mind Essentials, the Essential Selections from the Separate Transmission Record of the Dharma Collection with Personal Notes, the Treatise on the Perfect and Sudden Attainment of Buddhahood, the Treatise on Resolving Doubt in the Hua-tou, the Essential Gate of Buddha-Recitation, the Postscript to the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and others. His Dharma heirs included Huichen, Zhengxuan, Shouyu, and others.

[Full precepts] The complete and perfect precepts, such as the two hundred and fifty precepts of a monk and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts of a nun. [Monastic examination] The examination system for monastics implemented in Korea from the Goryeo period to the early Joseon dynasty. It was divided into the sectarian examination and the great examination. The sectarian examination was administered by the temples, while the great examination was administered by the state. Only those who passed the sectarian examination could take the great examination. The great examination was divided into a Chan-sect great examination and a doctrinal-sect great examination; the former was held at Gwangmyeong Temple, the chief temple of the Chan school, and the latter at Wangnyun Temple, the chief temple of the doctrinal school. The great examination was held once every three years. [Li Tongxuan (

)] Known in the world as Venerable Li, and also called the Great Adept of Jujube and Cypress, he was a Avatamsaka scholar of the Tang dynasty, a native of Cangzhou (present-day southeast of Cangxian, Hebei). In his youth he studied the principles of the Book of Changes; after the age of about forty he devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures, focusing deeply on the Avatamsaka Sutra. At that time the eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka had just been translated. In the spring of the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era (

), he carried the newly translated Avatamsaka Sutra to the home of Gao Shannu in Daxian Village, Tongying Township, southwest of Meng County in Taiyuan, and there composed a treatise to clarify the meaning of the scripture. For three years he never left the house; it is said that each day he ate only ten jujubes and one cypress-leaf cake in the morning, and so the world called him the Great Adept of Jujube and Cypress. He later carried his draft to an earthen shrine at the foot of Shenfushan (the earthen shrine at Fangshan, Shouyang, Taiyuan) to continue his writing, and after five years it was completed; this is the forty-fascicle New Avatamsaka Commentary. He then also wrote the four-fascicle Brief Explanation of the New Avatamsaka Sutra's Stages of Cultivation and Resolving Doubt. In the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era (
), though some say the twenty-eighth year of the Kaiyuan era (

), on the twenty-eighth day of the third month, he passed into nirvana at the age of ninety-six. [Avatamsaka Sutra] Its full title is the Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra of the Buddha, a central scripture in which, after his enlightenment at the Bodhimanda and elsewhere, the Buddha, by means of the great bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Manjushri, reveals the causal practice and resultant virtue of the Tathagata. This scripture has three Chinese translations: First, the translation by Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin, titled Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, in sixty fascicles; to distinguish it from the later Tang translation it is called the old translation of the Avatamsaka, or the sixty-fascicle Avatamsaka. Second, the translation by Shikshananda of the Tang era of Empress Wu Zetian, titled Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, in eighty fascicles, also called the new translation of the Avatamsaka, or the eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka. Third, the translation by Prajna in the Zhenyuan era of the Tang, also titled Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, in forty fascicles; its full title is the Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, the Conduct and Vows of Samantabhadra's Entry into the Inconceivable Realm of Liberation, abbreviated as the Conduct and Vows of Samantabhadra, or the forty-fascicle Avatamsaka.
[Direct Explanation of the True Mind]
In this essay, the true mind is what is generally called the self-nature. Direct explanation means speaking as it truly is, stating it plainly and straightforwardly.

The Direct Explanation of the True Mind treats the true mind (the self-nature) comprehensively from the following fifteen aspects: Right Faith in the True Mind, the Different Names of the True Mind, the Wondrous Essence of the True Mind, the Wondrous Function of the True Mind, Oneness and Difference of Essence and Function, the True Mind in Delusion, Pacifying False Thoughts of the True Mind, the Four Deportments of the True Mind, Where the True Mind Abides, the True Mind Beyond Death, the Principal and Auxiliary Practices, the Merits of the True Mind, Verifying the Merit of the True Mind, the True Mind Without Knowing, and Where the True Mind Goes. It illuminates the true mind (the self-nature) originally possessed by everyone, the root of delusion and awakening, and the path of cultivation and the realms of realization.
The Direct Explanation of the True Mind is a companion piece to the Cultivation of Mind Essentials (see
Annotated Cultivation of Mind Essentials

The self-nature is the essence, and the mind is the function of the self-nature. The mind has two states: the original mind and the cognitive mind. The original mind is the original state of the mind, luminous, clear, and profoundly translucent, standing alone and independent. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

'If you do not recognize the original mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If you recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, then you are called a great man, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.'
The cognitive mind is also called the
thought-discriminating mind

— the mind that arises by clinging to and discriminating the six objects of sense, which is what the Buddha calls the shadow cast by conditions of the six senses in the Sutra of Perfect Awakening. It is the mind that is present in our daily use, discriminating and knowing, that is, the thought of the present moment. Its characteristic is discrimination and calculation, delighting in one and rejecting the other. The arising of a thought, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing (the knowing here is the discriminating knowing) — these are all the working of the cognitive mind.
The original mind is undefiled, so it is also called the mind of pure self-nature. The original mind is without knowing yet knows everything, so the original mind is also called the
mind of numinous knowing

. It should be noted: the knowing of numinous knowing is the knowing of non-knowing; to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is called numinous knowing. The Record of the Mirror of the School says:
'Prajna is without knowing — it has no knowing that grasps marks.'
The Surangama Sutra says:
'To establish knowing upon views is the root of ignorance; when views no longer see, this is nirvana, the undefiled true purity.'
Cultivation is to still this scattered cognitive mind (the thought-discriminating mind) and thereby reach the state of the original mind (the mind of numinous knowing), as it is said:
'When the wild mind is not stilled, still it; when stilled, this is bodhi.'
. The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says:
'Still thought and forget
(let go of)
deliberation, and the Buddha himself appears before you.'
The Treasury of the Buddha-dharma Sutra says:
'The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is without thinking and without thought.'

Cultivation is to return to the source, to transform the state of the cognitive mind (the mind that discriminates by clinging to the six sense objects) into the state of the original mind (the empty, still, numinously knowing mind). To awaken is to awaken to this empty, still, numinously knowing mind; to cultivate is to guard this empty, still, numinously knowing mind. First protect, then let go, until reaching non-activity.
It should be noted, however, that in general discussions the essence and function, and the delusion and awakening, of the substance are often given separate names. For instance, the essay
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-garbha

, for the sake of convenience in discussion, gives separate names to the essence and function and to delusion and awakening of the substance: the self-nature is the essence, and the mind is its function. The state of the self-nature's awakening is called the original nature (the tathagata-garbha, the Buddha-nature); the state of the self-nature's delusion is called the cognitive nature (the store of cognition). The state of the mind's awakening is called the original mind (the true mind); the state of the mind's delusion is called the cognitive mind (the deluded mind). In the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, however, apart from an occasional use of the term deluded mind, it ordinarily uses only the term true mind, not distinguishing essence from function and using it for both delusion and awakening. On this point, chapter two, The Different Names of the True Mind, discriminates very clearly, and states:

'If one penetrates the true mind, all names are understood; if one is benighted about the true mind, all names are obstructed. Therefore, with regard to the true mind, one should look into it with care.'
Thus, whether the true mind in a given sentence refers to essence or function, delusion or awakening, should be discerned according to the context.
A note:
In the annotations, for ease of reading and understanding, when the quoted original text is rendered into plain language, quotation marks are likewise added. For example, the original text:
The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.'

And the annotated rendering: The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path, the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.' Therefore, the text within quotation marks in the annotations is not necessarily the original; readers are asked to note this.

blocks.text: 1. Right Faith in the True Mind

inline.s: [The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.' Again, the Consciousness-Only treatises say: 'Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can purify muddy water.' Thus, when all good things arise, faith leads the way. That is why Buddhist scriptures set 'Thus have I heard' at the beginning; this is what is meant by giving rise to faith.]

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path, the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.' Again, the Treatise on the Perfection of Consciousness Only says: 'Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can clarify muddy water.' Thus we know that when all good things arise, faith leads the way. That is why all Buddhist scriptures open with 'Thus have I heard' — precisely to lead readers to give rise to faith in the scriptures.
[Faith] To believe and to delight in. The faith in this passage refers to faith in the correct Dharma, and so it says:
'Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.'
It also says:
'Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can purify muddy water.'

[Roots of goodness] The good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, firm and unremovable, is called root. Again, good can produce wondrous fruits and give rise to further good, hence it is called root. [Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can purify muddy water] Faith in the correct Dharma is like the clear-water jewel that can clarify muddy water, able to purify the confused, deluded mind. [Clear-water jewel] As the saying goes: In the Western regions there is a treasure called the clear-water jewel. When this jewel is cast into muddy water, for every inch it enters, one inch of the muddy water becomes clear. As the jewel descends from inch to foot and to the bottom, all the muddy water accordingly becomes clear. [Thus have I heard] This is what I (Ananda) personally heard and saw (not what was passed on by hearsay). 'Thus have I heard' is a means of establishing trust, proving that this scripture is indeed spoken by the Buddha and that the recorded text is correct and without error. The 'I' in the phrase is the self-designation of Ananda, the compiler of the scripture. Ananda was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment. Later he left home under the Buddha and served as his attendant, being renowned for never forgetting what he heard, foremost in extensive learning. When Ananda left home, the Buddha had already taught for twenty years, so he asked the Buddha to repeat to him all that had been spoken before; at the same time, Ananda also attained the samadhi of the Self-Awakened Dharma-Nature, whereby he could fully penetrate all dharmas in concentration. Thus, after the Buddha's nirvana, when the Venerable Mahakashyapa assembled the canon at the Great Stone Cavern in the kingdom of Magadha, five hundred great arhats gathered together, and the assembly unanimously asked Ananda to ascend the seat and recite the scriptures.

[Someone asked: What difference is there between the faith of the ancestral school and the faith of the doctrinal school? Reply: There are several differences. The doctrinal school leads gods and men to have faith in cause and effect: those who love blessings and pleasures are taught to believe that the ten wholesome deeds are the wondrous cause and the realm of gods and men the pleasing fruit; those who delight in emptiness and stillness are taught to believe that the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing are the correct cause and the four noble truths (suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path) the noble fruit; those who delight in the fruit of Buddhahood are taught to believe that the six perfections over three incalculable eons are the great cause and the attainment of bodhi and nirvana the correct fruit.]

Question: What difference is there between the faith of the ancestral school (the patriarch school, Chan) and the faith of the doctrinal school (the text-based school)? Reply: There are several differences. The doctrinal school causes sentient beings in the human and heavenly realms to have faith in cause and effect: for those who love to enjoy blessings and pleasures, it tells them to believe that the ten wholesome deeds are the wondrous cause of blessings and pleasures, and birth as a human or god is the pleasing fruit; for those who delight in emptiness and stillness, it tells them to believe that the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing are the correct cause of emptiness and stillness, and the realization of the four noble truths (suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path) is the noble fruit; for those who delight in the fruit of Buddhahood, it tells them to believe that the wondrous practices of the six perfections over three incalculable eons are the great cause of becoming a Buddha, and the realization of bodhi and nirvana is the correct fruit.

[Doctrinal school] One that takes the scriptural teachings as the gate to the path. The Chan school calls itself the ancestral school (entering the path by the patriarchs' mind-to-mind transmission) and commonly calls other schools the doctrinal schools. [Four noble truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of its arising, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the true reality of actual life. Second, the arising in the truth of arising means to bring about, to cause; it explains the truth of how the suffering of life comes about. The suffering of life comes from clinging and craving that create karma, and so one undergoes suffering and transmigration. Third, the truth of cessation explains the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When all the arising of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, undefiled and unattached, one no longer undergoes suffering and transmigration; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the truth of the path explains how to forever cut off the arising of suffering (craving), that is, the path that extinguishes suffering — the noble eightfold path. Among the four noble truths, arising is the cause and suffering the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation the fruit. [Three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioned existence. The suffering of suffering: worldly people already have a body subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; added to this the oppression of many sufferings is truly suffering upon suffering, hence it is called the suffering of suffering. The suffering of decay is the suffering felt when a happiness that briefly appears is lost. The suffering of conditioned existence is the suffering of all conditioned things being impermanent, flowing on without rest and never settling. [Eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain at the time of birth; second, the suffering of old age, the pain of age and weakness; third, the suffering of illness, the pain of being sick; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the time of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the pain of parting from those one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting what one hates, the pain of meeting those one despises; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the pain of not getting what one wishes; eighth, the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates, that is, the fierce activity of the five aggregates covering the true nature.

[Noble eightfold path] Also called the eightfold correct path, the eight practices of the noble ones: first, right view, that is, correct understanding and vision; second, right thought, that is, correct reflection; third, right speech, that is, proper words; fourth, right action, that is, proper conduct; fifth, right livelihood, that is, a proper occupation and way of life; sixth, right effort, that is, correct striving; seventh, right mindfulness, that is, correct awareness; eighth, right concentration, that is, correct meditation. Cultivating this noble eightfold path, one can realize the fruit of arhatship. [Three incalculable eons] This is the time it takes a bodhisattva to cultivate to Buddhahood. The asankhyeya eon is translated in Chinese as countless long time. The stages by which a bodhisattva cultivates up to Buddhahood total fifty. Of these: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, forty stages in all, constitute the first incalculable eon; among the ten grounds, from the first ground to the seventh ground is the second incalculable eon; from the eighth ground to the tenth ground is the third incalculable eon. After the tenth ground one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

[The right faith of the ancestral school is not the same as the above. It does not believe in the cause and effect of all conditioned things; it merely requires believing that one is originally a Buddha: the true and spontaneous self-nature is fully possessed by everyone, and the wondrous essence of nirvana is perfected in each; one does not rely on seeking it elsewhere, for it has been complete all along. The Third Patriarch says: 'Round like the great void, lacking nothing and having nothing over; it is all because of grasping and rejecting, and so it is not thus.' Master Zhi says: 'Within the marked body there is the unmarked body; upon the road of ignorance there is the road of no-birth.' Yongjia says: 'The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya.' Therefore know that sentient beings are originally Buddha.]

The right faith of the ancestral school is not the same as the faith of the doctrinal school described above. The ancestral school does not believe in the cause and effect of all conditioned dharmas; it merely requires believing that one is originally a Buddha: the true and spontaneous self-nature is fully possessed by everyone, and the wondrous essence of nirvana is perfected in each; one does not rely on seeking it elsewhere, for it has been complete all along. The Third Patriarch of the Chan school, Sengcan, says: 'The true and spontaneous self-nature, round like the great void, lacking nothing and having nothing over — it is all on account of a mind of grasping and rejecting that the original nature does not appear (is not thus).' The Venerable Baozhi says: 'Within the marked body (the physical body) there is the unmarked body (the true mind); upon the road of ignorance there is the road of no-birth (the road of nirvana).' The Song of Realizing the Way by Master Yongjia says: 'The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya.' Therefore know that sentient beings are originally Buddha.

[Cause and effect of conditioned things] The cause and effect of conditioned dharmas. [Conditioned dharmas] All things that arise from the combination of causes and conditions. [Thusness] The true, unchanging nature of all things. This nature is extremely difficult to describe in words, and so the character 'thus' is used to represent it. The original nature is the real mark; the real mark is thusness, because it is non-dual, unchanging, immutable, and unmoving; the true face of all dharmas is the same single mark, and so it is called 'thus.' [Real mark] The true state of dharmas. 'The real mark of all dharmas' is the true state of all dharmas. In the

Buddha-Recitation Chapter, the second, of the Treasury of the Buddha-dharma Sutra, the Buddha says: 'What is called the real mark of all dharmas? That is to say, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without any being.' (For a detailed discussion of the real mark of all dharmas, see
The Real Mark of All Dharmas

one essay.) [The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya] This means: ignorance arises from the Buddha-nature (the true mind in delusion), and the physical body is a manifestation of the dharmakaya.

The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says: 'This one mind alone is the Buddha, and the Buddha and sentient beings are no different. But because sentient beings cling to marks and seek without, they lose it the more they seek; making the Buddha seek the Buddha, using the mind to grasp the mind, throughout eons and the whole of their lives they can never attain it. They do not know that when they still thought and forget (let go of) deliberation, the Buddha himself appears before them. This mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the sentient being. When one is a sentient being, this mind is not diminished; when one is a Buddha, this mind is not increased. Indeed, the six perfections and myriad practices and the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are originally complete in themselves, not depending on cultivation or addition; when conditions arise they are given forth, and when conditions cease they are still. If one is not resolved, and does not believe that this is the Buddha, but wishes to cultivate by clinging to marks to seek meritorious function, all of it is false thinking and runs counter to the path. This mind is the Buddha; there is no other Buddha, and no other mind. This mind is bright and pure, like empty space, with not a single mark. The moment one raises a thought, one departs from the essence of Dharma and clings to a mark; since beginnings there has never been a Buddha who clings to marks. To cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices seeking to become a Buddha is itself a ladder of stages; since beginnings there has never been a Buddha attained by stages.'

It also says: 'Apart from all marks, sentient beings and all Buddhas are not at all different; only when one can be without mind is that the ultimate. A student of the path, if he is not immediately without mind, though he cultivate through many eons will never accomplish the path, being bound by the practices of the three vehicles and unable to gain liberation. Yet the realization of this mind may be quick or slow. There are those who, on hearing the Dharma in a single thought, become without mind; there are those who reach it only at the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; and there are those who reach it only at the ten grounds. Whether it takes long or short, it is only upon becoming without mind that one abides; then there is nothing more to cultivate or realize. In truth there is nothing attained; this is real and not false. To attain it in a single thought and to attain it at the tenth ground are exactly the same in function, with no further depth or shallowness; it is only that through the eons one labors in vain.'

[Fifty-two stages] In going from an ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva passes through fifty-two stages in all: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment.
Q: The Chan school often says, '
See the mind and realize the nature,
and realizing the nature, become a Buddha.' What does this mean?
Answer:
See the mind and realize the nature
' means:

recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature. 'And realizing the nature, become a Buddha' means: having seen your own original nature, then cultivate in accord with the nature and perfectly fulfill the Buddha way.

Thus, 'see the mind and realize the nature, and realizing the nature become a Buddha' means: recognize your own original mind, see your own original nature, then cultivate in accord with the nature and perfectly fulfill the Buddha way. (See
Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

[Once right faith is born, it must be nourished with understanding. Yongming says: 'Faith without understanding increases ignorance; understanding without faith increases wrong views.' Therefore know that when faith and understanding are combined, one quickly enters the path.]

Once right faith is born, it must be nourished by understanding. Master Yongming says: 'Faith without understanding increases ignorance; understanding without faith increases wrong views.' Therefore know that when faith and understanding are combined, one can quickly enter the path (see the mind and realize the nature).

[Entering the path] Seeing the mind and realizing the nature. So far as the Chan school is concerned, before entering the path is the preliminary practice; after entering the path (sudden awakening) is the practice of cultivation (gradual cultivation); and after that is the realization of the path. The realm of realizing the path is as described in Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way. The Consciousness-Only school has a doctrine of five stages of cultivation: the stage of the equipment of merits, the stage of applied practice, the stage of clear penetration, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of ultimate attainment.

[Someone asked: If one has just given rise to the resolve of faith and has not yet entered the path, is there any benefit? Reply: The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: 'If a person, having heard this Dharma, gives rise to no timidity or weakness, know that such a person will certainly succeed to the Buddha-seed and will certainly be given the prophecy by all Buddhas. Even if a person could transform all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm and lead them to practice the ten wholesome deeds, it would not compare with a person who, in a single moment of thought, rightly ponders this Dharma; the merit of the latter surpasses the former beyond all comparison.' Again, the Prajna Sutra says: 'Those who, even in a single thought, give rise to pure faith, the Tathagata knows and sees them all; these sentient beings obtain such immeasurable blessings.']

Question: If one has just given rise to the resolve of faith (believing that one is originally a Buddha) and has not yet realized and entered the noble path, is there any benefit? Reply: The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: 'If a person, having heard this Dharma (that one is originally a Buddha), gives rise to no timidity or weakness, know that such a person is certainly a seed of Buddhahood and will certainly receive the prophecy from all Buddhas. Even if a person could deliver all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm and lead them to practice the ten wholesome deeds, it would not match a person who, in a single moment of thought, rightly ponders this Dharma (that one is originally a Buddha); the merit of the latter far exceeds the former and cannot be described.' Again, the Diamond Sutra (Vajracchedika Prajna Paramita Sutra) says: 'Those who, even in a single thought, give rise to pure faith, the Tathagata fully knows and sees them; these sentient beings obtain such immeasurable blessings.'
